case.title: Brownfield provider leakage
case.problem_statement: Qwen built-in voice knowledge appears in frontend, preflight, workflow, and root composition.
case.desired_outcome: Put voice discovery under one clear owner and reduce coordinated provider changes.
expected_future_changes: A second provider may be added.

confirmed_facts.text: A provider interface exists but does not own voice discovery.

clusters.title: Centralization of Voice Discovery and Provider Interface Stability
clusters.rationale: These forces represent a single architectural investigation into redefining the provider boundary: F1 identifies the immediate risk of metadata leakage, F3 establishes the functional requirement for an abstract interface to support future expansion, and F2 highlights the structural risks (change amplification) that must be managed when implementing this consolidation.

concern_analyses.concern: Centralization of Voice Discovery and Provider Interface Stability

findings.text: The constant `BUILT_IN_VOICES` is duplicated across multiple modules, including `provider.py`, `preflight.py`, and `frontend.py`.

Implementation details of the Qwen provider (specifically voice list constants) have leaked into high-level presentation and validation modules, suggesting that the boundary for `VoiceProvider` is not yet sufficiently opaque.

To achieve the goal of stability, moving the discovery logic entirely behind the `VoiceProvider` interface would consolidate change impact within the provider implementation, adhering to the need for localizing changes and avoiding coordinated edits across `preflight.py` and `frontend.py`.

implications: Structural risk: High potential for coordinated change amplification when adding new providers or updating voice sets.
Maintenance cost: Increased burden on maintainers to synchronize constant definitions across the dependency chain.

design_forces.title: Metadata Fragmentation
design_forces.description: The `BUILT_IN_VOICES` constant is identified in three separate modules (`provider.py`, `preflight.py`, and `frontend.py`). This creates a tension between the current state of distributed knowledge and the desired outcome of single-owner voice discovery, necessitating multi-module coordination for updates.
design_forces.importance: Critical: Directly drives the 'Brownfield provider leakage' problem and increases the risk of desynchronized module states.

design_forces.title: High-Impact Change Propagation
design_forces.description: The `provider.py` module exhibits a high structural proxy for change amplification (5 modules) and significant fan-in (4). This creates a tension where any modification to the provider's interface or core logic threatens to trigger cascading changes across the system.
design_forces.importance: High: This fragility makes the cost of evolution in the provider module disproportionately expensive relative to its local complexity.

design_forces.title: Provider Abstraction Requirement
design_forces.description: The identified future change (adding a second provider) creates a tension between the current `QwenProvider` implementation and the need for an interface that prevents implementation-specific details from leaking into higher-level modules like `workflow.py`. The exact degree of required indirection remains an unconfirmed requirement.
design_forces.importance: Medium: This structural pressure dictates whether the current provider-consumer relationship is sufficient or if a formal registry/plugin mechanism must be introduced.

alternatives.title: Maintain Distributed Definitions
alternatives.summary: Continue defining `BUILT_IN_VOICES` locally within each relevant module (`provider.py`, `preflight.py`, and `frontend.py`).

alternatives.title: Encapsulate Discovery via Interface
alternatives.summary: Shift the responsibility of voice availability to the `VoiceProvider` interface (e.g., through a `get_available_voices()` method), so that consumers query the provider at runtime rather than referencing static local constants.

alternatives.title: Centralized Constant Module
alternatives.summary: Move the `BUILT_IN_VOICES` constant to a single shared module/package that is imported by all dependent modules, effectively creating one source of truth for the list.

assumptions: The new provider will have its own unique set of available voices.
The addition of a provider should not require modifications to consumer modules like `preflight.py` or `frontend.py`.

alternative_results.alt_preserve_distributed_constants: Fails to meet stability goals; requires coordinated changes across the new provider module and all existing consumers to prevent inconsistent voice lists, leading to high change amplification.
alternative_results.alt_encapsulate_discovery: Provides maximum decoupling; by moving discovery to the `VoiceProvider` interface, only the new provider implementation needs modification, leaving consumer modules untouched.
alternative_results.alt_centralize_shared_constant: Reduces duplication but fails to resolve interface leakage; while it creates a single source of truth, adding a provider still requires updating the central module, which potentially maintains a dependency link between all providers and consumers.

scenarios.conclusion: Alternative A2 is the preferred architecture as it adheres to the principle of localizing change and achieves the desired outcome of opaque provider boundaries.

policy.title: Define interfaces around stable concepts, not incidental mechanisms
policy.body:
## Intent
Keep short-lived implementation choices from shaping long-lived application contracts.
## Guidance
Name domain capabilities and results independently from the first provider or framework.
## Signals
Public interfaces contain vendor names, transport fields, or framework lifecycle objects.
## Diagnostic questions
Would this concept still exist if the current implementation were replaced?
## Likely consequences
Contracts change for domain reasons rather than adapter churn.
## Exceptions
Provider-specific features may remain explicitly provider-specific when portability is not a goal.
## Positive example
`VoiceCatalog` represents an application capability while Qwen owns its construction.
## Counterexample
Renaming every concrete object to `Generic*` without changing its semantics.
## Related policies
See `contain-dependencies` and `keep-interfaces-simple`.

chunks.text: `VoiceCatalog` represents an application capability while Qwen owns its construction.

policy.title: Keep each architectural fact in one authoritative place
policy.body:
## Intent
Prevent one conceptual change from requiring synchronized edits.
## Guidance
Consolidate duplicated rules, mappings, and capability knowledge under their natural owner.
## Signals
The same list, constant, validation rule, or conditional appears in unrelated modules.
## Diagnostic questions
Are these copies accidental, cached, or intentionally independent?
## Likely consequences
Changes become atomic and contradictory definitions are less likely.
## Exceptions
Deliberate denormalization is valid when synchronization and ownership are explicit.
## Positive example
Built-in voices are declared by the provider and consumed by preflight and presentation.
## Counterexample
Unrelated code is merged merely because two fragments happen to look alike.
## Related policies
See `explicit-source-of-truth` and `assign-clear-ownership`.

chunks.text: Built-in voices are declared by the provider and consumed by preflight and presentation.

policy.title: Hide implementation details behind the owning boundary

source.author: ArchCompass
inspiration: John Ousterhout, A Philosophy of Software Design

policy.body:
## Intent
Prevent callers from depending on decisions that belong to another module.
## Guidance
Expose the capability a caller needs while keeping formats, provider rules, and algorithms private.
## Signals
Several callers reproduce the same internal rule or inspect an implementation-specific type.
## Diagnostic questions
Which decisions can the module change without coordinating with callers?
## Likely consequences
Callers become simpler and implementation changes affect fewer locations.
## Exceptions
Transparent data types are appropriate when their representation is the stable shared concept.
## Positive example
A provider returns a voice catalog without exposing how its built-in voices are discovered.
## Counterexample
A wrapper forwards every provider option and therefore hides nothing.
## Related policies
See `assign-clear-ownership` and `contain-dependencies`.

chunks.text: A provider returns a voice catalog without exposing how its built-in voices are discovered.

policy.title: Apply consistency where it reduces interpretation cost
policy.body:
## Intent
Make similar concepts behave similarly without forcing unlike responsibilities into one pattern.
## Guidance
Standardize naming, error handling, and lifecycle conventions at genuine shared boundaries.
## Signals
Equivalent operations use different terminology or error semantics without a domain reason.
## Diagnostic questions
Are the cases conceptually alike, and what does consistency let a maintainer infer?
## Likely consequences
Existing knowledge transfers and surprising special cases decline.
## Exceptions
Different domain semantics should remain visibly different.
## Positive example
All repositories use the same not-found and revision-conflict semantics.
## Counterexample
Every component is forced through one base class despite different ownership and lifecycle.
## Related policies
See `make-relationships-discoverable` and `keep-interfaces-simple`.

policy.title: Give each layer a distinct abstraction

source.author: ArchCompass
inspiration: John Ousterhout, A Philosophy of Software Design (2nd ed.)

policy.body:
## Intent
Ensure that an additional layer hides, translates, or consolidates complexity instead of merely adding another name and call hop.
## Guidance
Make each layer express concepts appropriate to its responsibility. A layer should aggregate operations, enforce invariants, translate representations, or otherwise provide a simpler view than the layer below it; collapse layers that only repeat another interface.
## Signals
Methods mostly forward the same arguments to similarly named methods and return the same result, or adjacent interfaces expose nearly identical concepts and sequencing.
## Diagnostic questions
What knowledge or decision does this layer hide, and could its caller use the lower-level interface with essentially the same understanding?
## Likely consequences
Call paths become shorter, interfaces earn their maintenance cost, and each remaining layer provides a meaningful place for change.
## Exceptions
A deliberately transparent adapter, decorator, security boundary, or compatibility seam may mirror an interface when isolation itself has concrete value and the extra hop remains obvious.
## Positive example
A repository exposes a domain aggregate assembled from storage rows, while the application service exposes a complete use-case result rather than forwarding row-oriented operations.
## Counterexample
A controller calls a service that calls a client with the same method name, parameters, and result, with no validation, translation, policy, or aggregation at either boundary.
## Related policies
See `prefer-deep-modules`, `keep-interfaces-simple`, and `contain-dependencies`.

policy.title: Keep one conceptual change local
policy.body:
## Intent
Reduce coordinated edits caused by a single decision.
## Guidance
Group knowledge that changes together while separating responsibilities that change independently.
## Signals
Adding one provider requires changes in presentation, validation, workflow, and root composition.
## Diagnostic questions
Which files change together, and is there one responsibility behind those edits?
## Likely consequences
Feature changes touch fewer locations and partial updates become less likely.
## Exceptions
Cross-cutting security or compliance changes may intentionally affect many boundaries.
## Positive example
Adding a provider requires one adapter and one composition registration.
## Counterexample
A large central module is justified only because all changes are now in one file.
## Related policies
See `avoid-duplicated-knowledge` and `contain-dependencies`.

chunks.text: Adding one provider requires changes in presentation, validation, workflow, and root composition.

uncertainty: Static call resolution is conservative and runtime behavior is not observed.
